paras: The lynching of Tom Hall was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Wickliffe, Ballard County, Kentucky, at about 1 a.m. on October 16, 1903. Hall was accused of shooting Crockett Childress, a white youth, in a fight over the railroad platform at Kevil five nights earlier, a charge he denied. Papers across the country remarked on how quietly the mob had worked; no arrests were reported.

Kevil was a small Illinois Central station about ten miles from Paducah. According to a Paducah dispatch, a fight there on the night of October 11 "originated over the negroes ordering the white people to remain off their part of the railroad platform"; Hall was shot through the arm and Childress near the heart. Afterward men around Kevil armed themselves, and Black residents left until, by one report, none could be found.

Held at Paducah, Hall told the Sun he had done no shooting and named Jim Rivers, who had since left Kevil. On October 15 Sheriff Lee Potter took him to Wickliffe and turned him over to Jailer Z. T. Dulworth.

At about 1 a.m. Dulworth answered a knock at his residence beside the jail and, by the Sun's account, faced "about half a hundred masked men". A spokesman demanded Hall, and the jailer gave him up; the Spokane Press said the men forced him to hand over the keys. One man struck Hall on the head with a pistol, and the leaders refused to hear his explanation, saying they "intended to have justice done."

In the jail yard the mob hanged Hall from a walnut branch while members held the jailer back, then dispersed so quietly that nearby residents did not know a lynching had taken place. The Sun said Hall "died game," while the Spokane and St. Louis papers said he begged for his life and a Kentucky wire said he died "protesting his innocence."

Coroner Dan Enlow cut the body down for burial in the potter's field. A Kentucky wire said only that "The usual verdict was rendered"; no report of an inquest's findings, an arrest or grand jury action appears in the coverage. The Sun wrote that the Wickliffe authorities had made no special effort to learn the leaders, supposed to be friends of Childress, while the St. Louis Republic said they were white men from near Kevil.

Childress died on October 20, and the Sun's report of his death said "it is claimed Tom Hall shot" him. A Kevil dispatch of October 19 said Black people there had threatened Childress and that white citizens were ready to resist.

The Paducah Sun headlined the lynching "Orderly Mob Swooped Down on the Wickliffe Jail," with the subhead "Hall Claimed to Be Innocent," and quoted the jailer that "a more orderly body of men could not have been formed for such a purpose."

A brief Wickliffe wire giving the mob as 100 men and noting Hall's denial ran from Washington to South Dakota between October 16 and 22, and Kentucky weeklies used a Paducah version with 25 masked men. The Spokane Press ran the harshest account, "Brutal Negro Meets Death at Rope's End," calling the shooting "unprovoked," while the St. Louis Republic called the victim "Hawes." The Indianapolis Journal quoted a dispatch calling it "one of the quickest and quietest lynchings that ever occurred in western Kentucky," and the Salt Lake Herald noted that no race riot followed because "All the negroes left town."

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal on October 17 blamed the "color line separations which are in vogue in the South" for the Kevil trouble and wrote that the area's Afro-Americans "have had to flee for their lives," without mentioning the lynching. The Chicago Broad Ax listed Hall in a year-end lynching chronology.

The mob was put at 25 by a Paducah wire, 28 by the St. Louis Republic, about fifty by the Sun and 100 by the Wickliffe wire. Whether Hall fired the shot was contested: he named Jim Rivers, while Childress and Manard Reed identified him. The St. Paul Appeal blamed the segregated platform for the fight, and the Spokane Press called the shooting unprovoked.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Hall
bases: A masked mob took Hall, a Black prisoner accused of shooting a white youth, from the Wickliffe jail and hanged him (A5, A7, A28).

Hall was hanged by a mob variously numbered at 25 to 100 that overpowered the jailer and took him from custody, its leaders saying they 'intended to have justice done' for the shooting of Childress (A5, A7, A28, A11).

The local Paducah Sun, an independent Cairo special to the St. Louis Republic, and two separate wire stories (Wickliffe and Paducah datelines) agree that a mob took Hall from the Wickliffe jail and hanged him (A5, A11, A7, A28).

accounts.gist: About fifty masked men woke the jailer at 1 a.m., took Hall, struck him with a pistol and hanged him from a walnut tree in the jail yard; the mob was 'orderly' and dispersed.

accounts.label: Wickliffe wire
accounts.gist: A mob of 100 took Hall from jail and hanged him in the jail yard; Hall denied wounding Childress and blamed another Black man.

accounts.label: Paducah wire (Kentucky papers)
accounts.gist: Twenty-five masked men overpowered Jailer Taylor Dulworth; Hall died protesting his innocence; 'The usual verdict was rendered.'

accounts.label: Cairo special to the St. Louis Republic
accounts.gist: Twenty-eight white men from near Kevil rode in, forced the jailer to give up 'Hawes' and hanged him in the Courthouse Square as he begged for his life.

accounts.label: Spokane Press (Paducah dateline)
accounts.gist: An 'infuriated mob' hanged 'Bob Douglas', a 'brutal negro' whose shooting of the boy was 'unprovoked'.

accounts.label: Black editorial (St. Paul Appeal)
accounts.gist: The Kevil fight came from separate platform sections for Black and white passengers; Afro-Americans of the area had to flee.

framing.detail: Paducah Sun headlined 'Orderly Mob Swooped Down on the Wickliffe Jail' and 'Hall Claimed to Be Innocent', called the Kevil fight a 'miniature race war' and Hall 'a desperate negro'.
Wickliffe wire under heads such as 'Lynched in Jail Yard', 'Negro Is Lynched', 'Mob Hangs Negro', noting Hall's denial.
Kentucky papers ran 'Colored Man Lynched. A Mob of 25 Strung Him Up For Shooting a White Boy.'
Spokane Press: 'Brutal Negro Meets Death at Rope's End'; the crime 'unprovoked'.
Indianapolis Journal and Salt Lake Herald editorial quips on Kentucky's record and on Black residents leaving town.
St. Paul Appeal blamed 'color line separations' for the Kevil trouble; no comment on the lynching found.
Chicago Broad Ax listed Hall in a year-end lynching chronology.
